step_title: Halt all new low-margin sales immediately
step_description: Identify and stop accepting orders below 20% gross margin. Calculate your break-even GM% using fixed costs divided by revenue and enforce it as a hard floor for all new business. Every below-threshold sale erodes cash faster than no sale at all.

step_title: Perform emergency COGS line-item audit now
step_description: Pull three months of COGS invoices and categorise every line by supplier and volume. Identify the top five cost drivers that represent 80% of COGS. You cannot fix what you have not explicitly mapped.

step_title: Call top three suppliers for emergency renegotiation
step_description: Contact your three largest suppliers within 48 hours and request a 10–15% temporary price reduction or extended payment terms. Present your volume commitment — most suppliers prefer a discounted deal to losing a client entirely.

step_title: Reprice top three products by 8–15% immediately
step_description: Increase prices on your three highest-volume products right now. In most SME contexts, 70% of customers will not object to a meaningful price increase if value is communicated clearly. Test with a subset first, then roll out broadly.

step_title: Eliminate the five lowest-margin product lines
step_description: Rank all products or services by gross margin percentage and remove the bottom five from your active offering. Redirect freed capacity, working capital, and sales attention toward higher-margin lines. Fewer but more profitable products is almost always right at this stage.

step_title: Cancel or pause all non-essential supplier contracts
step_description: Review every supplier and sub-contractor agreement and immediately pause any non-essential service. For essential suppliers, request a 60-90 day payment deferral. Target a 10% reduction in total COGS within 30 days.

step_title: Introduce cost-plus pricing model for all quotes
step_description: Build a simple pricing template that calculates the minimum acceptable price for each job or product. Set the floor at your break-even GM% plus a 10% buffer and make this a non-negotiable rule before any quote is issued.

step_title: Audit and eliminate production waste above 3% of COGS
step_description: Measure waste, scrap, and rework as a percentage of COGS. A 2–3% reduction in waste directly improves gross margin by the same amount. Assign accountability to one person and set a 30-day reduction target.

step_title: Redesign sales commissions to reward margin not revenue
step_description: Pay commissions on gross profit, not gross revenue. Salespeople paid on revenue will discount aggressively; salespeople paid on margin will protect pricing. Model the change using the last six months of sales data before implementing.

step_title: Assess vertical integration for your largest cost input
step_description: Identify your single largest COGS input and assess whether partial vertical integration — owning supply, manufacturing in-house, or a joint venture — could reduce cost by more than 15%. This structural play can permanently shift your margin floor.

step_title: Rank all products by gross margin percentage now
step_description: Generate a ranked list of all products or services by gross margin percentage. Identify the bottom 20% of SKUs — these are dragging your overall margin down. Document revenue and margin contribution of each before making changes.

step_title: Audit discount patterns by salesperson and customer
step_description: Pull all discounts, rebates, and credit notes issued in the last six months and attribute them by salesperson and customer account. Discounting is often the primary reason gross margin erodes quietly. Set a maximum 5% discount authority without manager approval.

step_title: Renegotiate your three largest supplier contracts now
step_description: Prepare a negotiation pack showing 12-month purchase history, payment record, and projected volumes. Request a 5–10% price reduction or volume rebate. Even modest reductions compound significantly at scale over 12 months.

step_title: Set and enforce minimum gross margin per product category
step_description: Define a minimum acceptable gross margin percentage for each product or service category and enforce it as pricing policy. Any sale below this floor requires sign-off from the owner or CFO. Communicate the rationale clearly to your sales team.

step_title: Test a 5–8% price increase on lowest-elasticity products
step_description: Identify products where customers are least price-sensitive — essential, differentiated, or hard-to-replace offerings. Test a 5–8% price increase with 20% of customers and monitor churn over 30 days before rolling out broadly.

step_title: Redirect 30% of sales effort toward highest-margin products
step_description: Analyse your sales team time allocation against the margin profile of what they sell. Use spiffs, targets, or simplified quoting tools to make high-margin products easier to sell. This mix shift improves overall margin without changing prices.

step_title: Set up monthly gross margin reporting by product line
step_description: Create a simple dashboard tracking gross margin percentage by product line, updated monthly. Share this report with your sales and operations leads. What gets measured and discussed is what gets managed.

step_title: Qualify two alternative suppliers for your largest cost input
step_description: Introduce competitive tension by qualifying two alternative suppliers for your largest COGS input. Even if you do not switch, having alternatives gives you leverage to negotiate better terms with your incumbent. Aim for a 5–8% cost reduction over 90 days.

step_title: Develop a premium tier for your best-selling product
step_description: Design a higher-value variant of your best-selling product with enhanced features or service levels that justifies a 15–25% premium. Premium tiers improve overall portfolio margin without disrupting your existing volume base.

step_title: Explore outsourcing high-cost low-differentiation inputs
step_description: Assess whether any component of your production or delivery process can be outsourced to a specialist at lower cost than in-house. Focus on high-cost, low-differentiation activities. Even a 10% reduction in one major input line adds 2–3 percentage points to gross margin.

step_title: Benchmark gross margin against industry top quartile
step_description: Research gross margin ranges for your sector and compare your current margin to the top quartile, not the average. If you are below the top quartile, you have a specific improvement target to work toward.

step_title: Introduce value-based pricing for premium customers
step_description: Review your top 20% of customers by profitability and assess whether your pricing reflects the full value you deliver. Value-based pricing anchored to customer outcomes is the most sustainable route to gross margins above 60% in most service businesses.

step_title: Formalise annual supplier renegotiation cycle
step_description: Set a calendar reminder to renegotiate all major supplier contracts annually, 90 days before renewal. Use your growth trajectory and payment history as leverage. Even 2–3% per year in input cost reduction compounds to a significant margin advantage over three years.

step_title: Launch cross-sell and upsell programme for existing customers
step_description: Design two or three upsell or cross-sell offerings for your existing customer base. Selling to existing customers costs 5–7x less than acquiring new ones, and higher basket values typically carry higher margins due to lower incremental fulfilment costs.

step_title: Develop a premium product tier with 25–40% price uplift
step_description: Create a high-value variant of your best-selling product commanding a 25–40% price premium. Premium tiers serve your most demanding customers and lift overall portfolio margin without disrupting the existing volume base.

step_title: Conduct six-monthly product rationalisation reviews
step_description: Formally review your catalogue every six months and retire any SKU generating below your target gross margin that has not grown in two consecutive periods. Product complexity in low-margin lines is a silent drag on operational efficiency.

step_title: Invest in automation to reduce direct labour in COGS
step_description: Map your production or service delivery process and identify the most labour-intensive steps. Research automation options that could reduce direct labour by 15–25%. Model the payback period before committing capital.

step_title: Build a monthly gross margin waterfall report
step_description: Create a monthly waterfall chart showing gross margin movement from prior period — broken into pricing changes, volume changes, product mix shifts, and cost changes. This visibility allows proactive management before margin becomes a problem.

step_title: Negotiate exclusive or preferred supplier agreements
step_description: Pursue preferred supplier status or exclusivity agreements with two or three key suppliers in exchange for volume commitments. These agreements typically yield 5–12% better pricing than spot purchasing and reduce supply chain risk simultaneously.

step_title: Build an intellectual property or brand moat to protect margin
step_description: Assess whether patents, trademarks, trade secrets, or strong brand positioning could protect your margin premium from competitive erosion. Gross margin above the industry median is only sustainable if defended by a durable competitive advantage.

step_title: Freeze all non-critical direct cost commitments today
step_description: Place an immediate hold on all new purchase orders and supplier commitments. Only release orders where production would stop without them. Your COGS-to-revenue ratio is unsustainable and every new commitment at current margins deepens the problem.

step_title: Map every direct cost to a specific product or job
step_description: Create a cost card for your top five revenue sources attributing every direct cost to specific output. This will reveal which products are consuming disproportionate COGS and whether your cost allocation assumptions are still accurate.

step_title: Call top five suppliers for emergency price reduction
step_description: Schedule calls with your five largest suppliers this week and request an emergency 10–20% reduction or 90-day payment deferral. Frame it as a survival conversation — most long-term suppliers prefer a discounted relationship to losing a client.

step_title: Eliminate all subcontractor markups above market rate
step_description: Identify every subcontracted service and calculate the markup as a proportion of COGS. Either renegotiate the rate, bring it in-house, or eliminate it. Subcontractor markup of 20–40% is common and often invisible until costs are explicitly mapped.

step_title: Suspend your two lowest-margin products immediately
step_description: Stop producing and selling your two lowest-margin offerings now. Use the freed capacity, cash, and management attention to scale your highest-margin products. A focused product range is almost always more profitable for an SME under cost pressure.

step_title: Measure and cut material waste to below 3% of COGS
step_description: Assign a team member to physically audit your production process for waste, scrap, rework, and over-ordering. Set a target of reducing waste to below 3% of COGS within 30 days and document each waste source with its monetary value.

step_title: Implement purchase order approval for all COGS spend
step_description: Require a mandatory purchase order for all direct cost commitments above a low threshold. This single control prevents rogue spending, creates audit trails, and immediately reduces impulse procurement that inflates COGS.

step_title: Pass direct cost increases through to customers immediately
step_description: Review all long-term contracts for escalation clauses. If your input costs have risen but prices have not followed, you are absorbing the inflation. Notify customers of price increases within 30 days with a clear cost-justification narrative.

step_title: Consolidate suppliers by 30% to earn volume discounts
step_description: Reduce your active supplier count by 30–40% and concentrate spend with preferred suppliers. Consolidated purchasing typically yields volume discounts of 5–15%. Review your supplier list and identify candidates for consolidation within 60 days.

step_title: Build monthly COGS variance reporting with owner accountability
step_description: Establish a monthly direct cost budget broken down by category — materials, labour, subcontractors, freight. Review actual versus budget monthly with your operations lead. Sustained discipline over direct costs separates healthy SMEs from struggling ones.

step_title: Benchmark direct cost ratio against your industry peers
step_description: Research COGS-to-revenue ratios for your sector — manufacturing typically 50–70%, services 20–40%, retail 60–75%. Knowing where you stand relative to peers gives you a specific improvement target rather than an abstract goal.

step_title: Isolate the three largest COGS cost drivers
step_description: Analyse your profit and loss and isolate the three largest categories within direct costs. For most businesses 80% of COGS sits in three to five line items. Concentrated effort on these categories will have a disproportionate impact on overall margin.

step_title: Solicit competitive quotes from two alternative suppliers
step_description: For your two largest direct cost inputs, obtain formal quotes from alternative suppliers. You do not need to switch — benchmarking creates negotiating leverage with your current supplier. Even a 5% reduction in your top two COGS inputs can meaningfully shift direct cost ratio.

step_title: Measure and improve direct labour productivity by 10%
step_description: Calculate output per direct labour hour across your main production or service activities. Compare to prior periods and industry benchmarks. A 10% improvement in labour productivity reduces direct labour as a percentage of COGS by a similar proportion.

step_title: Implement formal procurement policy for all direct purchases
step_description: Establish written procurement rules: minimum two quotes for purchases above R10 000; annual renegotiation of supplier contracts above R50 000; mandatory purchase orders for all COGS commitments. Procurement discipline typically yields 5–10% cost reduction within six months.

step_title: Reduce waste rate to below 2% of direct material costs
step_description: Measure your current waste and scrap rate as a percentage of total direct material costs. Implement a visual management system to flag and record waste daily. Target a reduction to below 2% within 90 days and track progress weekly.

step_title: Negotiate annual volume rebates with top three suppliers
step_description: Propose annual volume rebates to your three largest suppliers — typically 2–5% of spend returned at year-end if volume commitments are met. These rebates are common but rarely offered proactively; you need to request them explicitly.

step_title: Align direct labour scheduling with revenue-generating activity
step_description: Analyse your direct labour roster against production or delivery volume. Identify periods of low utilisation and shift scheduling to align labour costs more closely with revenue activity. This reduces the fixed component of what should be a variable cost.

step_title: Run a lean improvement sprint on your highest-cost process
step_description: Select your single highest direct-cost process and apply a focused lean methodology: map the steps, identify non-value-adding activities, and eliminate them. A 2-week lean sprint can typically reduce process costs by 10–20%.

step_title: Lock in fixed-price supplier agreements for cost certainty
step_description: For your three largest cost inputs, assess whether a 12–24 month fixed-price agreement provides savings versus spot purchasing. Price certainty also aids financial planning and reduces the risk of margin compression from input cost inflation.

step_title: Document cost management practices as standard procedures
step_description: Write your current direct cost controls, supplier management practices, and procurement rules as formal SOPs. This protects current performance from erosion when staff change and provides a baseline for continuous improvement.

step_title: Build a direct cost early warning system
step_description: Set up monthly monitoring with an alert threshold — trigger a review if COGS/Revenue rises more than 2 percentage points above your current level in any single month. Early detection prevents small cost increases from compounding into margin crises.

step_title: Develop strategic sourcing partnerships with key suppliers
step_description: Move your most critical suppliers from transactional to strategic relationships. Share your growth plans and purchase forecasts in exchange for preferred pricing, priority supply, and joint cost reduction initiatives. Strategic partnerships can yield 8–15% long-term cost advantages.

step_title: Invest in technology to reduce direct labour intensity
step_description: Identify your most labour-intensive direct cost activities and research technology that could automate or semi-automate them. Calculate ROI based on labour savings over three years. In many SME contexts, payback periods of 18–36 months are achievable.

step_title: Explore joint purchasing with complementary peer businesses
step_description: Connect with two or three non-competing businesses in your sector to negotiate collective purchasing with shared suppliers. Pooled procurement achieves pricing typically reserved for much larger buyers, reducing direct costs by 5–10% without changing your model.

step_title: Create a staff cost-reduction suggestion programme
step_description: Launch a formal suggestion programme for operations staff with financial rewards for implemented cost-reduction ideas. Frontline workers have the best insights into waste and inefficiency. Target a 1–2% annual improvement in direct cost ratio through this channel.

step_title: Conduct make-versus-buy analysis for major cost inputs
step_description: Formally analyse your largest direct cost inputs to assess whether in-house production, partial manufacture, or vertical integration could reduce cost below current market pricing. Revisit this analysis every two to three years as your scale evolves.

step_title: Include direct cost benchmarking in annual business planning
step_description: Make an explicit direct cost benchmarking exercise part of your annual planning cycle. Compare your COGS structure against industry data and best-in-class operators. Use benchmarks to set your cost targets for the coming year.

step_title: Assess local sourcing to reduce supply chain cost and risk
step_description: If any major direct cost inputs are imported or sourced from distant suppliers, assess local or regional alternatives. This reduces currency exposure, freight costs, and supply disruption risk — all contributors to direct cost stability and predictability.

step_title: Publish a three-year direct cost improvement roadmap
step_description: Create a structured plan to reduce your direct cost ratio by a further 3–5 percentage points over three years. Identify the specific initiatives — technology, supplier strategy, process improvement, and product mix — driving each percentage point. Review quarterly.

step_title: List every fixed cost and classify it immediately
step_description: Within 24 hours write out every fixed cost with its monthly amount, contract end date, and whether it is essential to operations. This mapping is your cost reduction hit list. Do not attempt to cut costs without completing this exercise first.

step_title: Cancel or pause all non-essential fixed-cost contracts now
step_description: Immediately cancel or pause every fixed cost that is not critical to generating revenue — subscriptions, memberships, non-essential software, discretionary retainers. Target a 20% reduction in fixed costs within the first two weeks.

step_title: Negotiate rent reduction or rental holiday with landlord
step_description: Contact your landlord this week and request a 3–6 month rental reduction or deferral. South African commercial landlords faced significant vacancies post-2020 and many will negotiate rather than lose a tenant. A 20% reduction for 6 months saves meaningful cash.

step_title: Freeze all hiring and implement salary review freeze
step_description: Place an immediate freeze on all new hires. Review all employment contracts for salary review clauses and defer discretionary increases. Payroll is typically the largest fixed cost in a service business — protecting it from further growth is essential in a crisis.

step_title: Calculate your operational break-even revenue today
step_description: Divide total monthly fixed costs by your gross margin percentage to find minimum monthly revenue required to achieve positive operating margin. This number must drive all revenue decisions for the next 90 days.

step_title: Renegotiate financing and lease payments with your bank
step_description: Contact your bank or asset finance provider and request a 3–6 month capital repayment holiday or payment restructuring. Banks are significantly more flexible with businesses that proactively contact them before missing payments.

step_title: Convert fixed costs to variable costs wherever possible
step_description: Identify fixed cost lines that could be restructured as variable or output-based — switch from salaried roles to contractor arrangements, fixed retainers to usage-based pricing, or negotiate revenue-share agreements with suppliers.

step_title: Generate revenue to absorb fixed costs via capacity utilisation
step_description: Drive revenue using current resources: reactivate dormant customers, cross-sell to existing accounts, accelerate the pipeline on deals near closing. Additional revenue from existing capacity adds to operating margin at a very high incremental rate since fixed costs are already covered.

step_title: Sublease unused office or production space immediately
step_description: If you have spare office, warehouse, or production space, list it for sublease immediately. Even recovering 30–50% of your rental cost through a sublease is meaningful cash recovery. Many Cape Town and Johannesburg SMEs find subtenants within 4–8 weeks.

step_title: Build a 12-month fixed cost reduction plan with milestones
step_description: Once immediate cuts are made, build a structured plan for the next 12 months identifying each fixed cost contract due for renewal, the target reduction percentage, and the responsible owner. Sustained management of fixed costs requires a plan, not just a reaction.

step_title: Calculate your operational break-even revenue today
step_description: Divide total monthly fixed costs by your gross margin percentage to get the revenue needed just to cover fixed costs. Compare this to your current and forecasted monthly revenue. The gap — positive or negative — defines your urgency and your target.

step_title: Audit fixed cost contracts for renewal opportunities
step_description: List all fixed cost contracts with renewal or renegotiation dates. Contracts coming up for renewal in the next six months should be renegotiated proactively. Target a 10–15% reduction using your payment history as leverage.

step_title: Cancel the five lowest-value fixed-cost subscriptions
step_description: Review every software subscription, service contract, and ongoing fixed commitment. Cancel the five that deliver the least value relative to their cost. Most businesses are paying for three to five services that are rarely or never used.

step_title: Negotiate office or facility costs down by 10–15%
step_description: Approach your landlord or facilities provider with a market comparison of current rental rates in your area and a proposal for a rent reduction or lease restructuring. The risk of losing a tenant is a powerful incentive for most commercial landlords to negotiate.

step_title: Implement a revenue growth plan to dilute fixed cost ratio
step_description: The fixed cost ratio improves both by reducing costs and by growing revenue. Identify the fastest route to a 10–15% revenue increase using existing capacity — pricing, activation of dormant customers, or new channels — without adding fixed costs.

step_title: Review headcount for roles without clear revenue linkage
step_description: Map every staff role to a revenue or operational outcome. Roles without a clear link to value creation should be restructured, reassigned, or eliminated. This is about ensuring every fixed cost has a visible return.

step_title: Explore shared services or outsourcing for non-core functions
step_description: Identify non-core functions — accounting, HR, IT support, legal — where outsourcing to a shared services provider would cost less than maintaining fixed in-house headcount. In South Africa, outsourced bookkeeping costs R3 000–R8 000 per month versus R20 000+ in-house.

step_title: Replace fixed retainers with output-based agreements
step_description: Review all fixed monthly retainer arrangements and propose converting them to output-based or project-based billing. This converts a fixed cost to a variable one and aligns supplier payment with actual value delivered.

step_title: Benchmark fixed cost structure against similar-sized businesses
step_description: Research what fixed cost ratios are typical for businesses at your revenue scale in your sector. Industry associations and financial benchmarking databases publish this data. Use the comparison to identify which specific fixed cost categories are above peer levels.

step_title: Build a scalable cost structure ahead of revenue growth
step_description: As you plan growth, design your fixed cost structure to scale at a lower rate than revenue. Adopt variable or commission-based compensation, flexible facility arrangements, and cloud-based or usage-priced technology — so your fixed cost ratio improves as you grow.

step_title: Review fixed cost structure for efficiency every six months
step_description: Schedule a semi-annual fixed cost review assessing each major expense for value delivered. Cancel or renegotiate any fixed cost that cannot be directly linked to a revenue or operational outcome. This discipline prevents healthy cost structures from drifting upward through inertia and contract auto-renewals.

step_title: Set a fixed cost ceiling as percentage of revenue
step_description: Define a maximum acceptable fixed cost ratio for your business and enforce it as a financial policy. If fixed costs approach the ceiling as revenue fluctuates, trigger a review before the ratio deteriorates. Having a ceiling converts good performance from luck into managed discipline.

step_title: Negotiate multi-year fixed cost agreements at current rates
step_description: Lock in your current favourable fixed cost rates with landlords, key suppliers, and service providers through multi-year agreements. Securing 2–3 year terms now protects you from inflation-driven cost increases and preserves your current ratio. Offer prompt payment or volume commitments in exchange for rate certainty.

step_title: Build an operating leverage model before any headcount addition
step_description: Before adding any fixed headcount, model the revenue required to maintain your current fixed cost ratio. Each new permanent hire increases your break-even revenue requirement. This model ensures growth-driven hiring does not silently erode your cost structure.

step_title: Transition non-core roles to variable cost arrangements
step_description: Identify functions that are not core to your competitive advantage — IT support, HR administration, marketing execution — and assess whether outsourcing or contractor arrangements would reduce fixed exposure. Even partial conversion of 10–15% of fixed payroll to variable cost meaningfully improves resilience during revenue dips.

step_title: Stress-test your cost structure against a 20% revenue decline
step_description: Model what happens to profitability and cash if revenue drops 20% for three consecutive months. Identify which fixed costs become unsustainable and what decisions you would make first. Completing this exercise in advance of a crisis means you act faster and more decisively if it occurs.

step_title: Invest fixed cost savings into revenue-generating capacity
step_description: Where fixed cost reductions are achieved, redirect the savings into sales, marketing, or product development rather than allowing them to be absorbed elsewhere. This compounds the benefit — lower fixed cost ratio AND higher revenue — creating a virtuous cycle of improving operating leverage.

step_title: Benchmark your fixed cost ratio against top-quartile industry peers
step_description: Identify the fixed cost ratio of the top-quartile performers in your sector using industry reports, financial benchmarking databases, or peer comparisons through your industry association. Even a healthy ratio may have room to improve if the best operators in your sector are running leaner.

step_title: Design your next growth phase on a scalable cost architecture
step_description: As you plan your next stage of growth, deliberately architect fixed costs to scale at a slower rate than revenue. Adopt cloud-based or usage-priced technology, flexible facility arrangements, and performance-linked compensation structures so that operating leverage improves as revenue grows.

step_title: Include fixed cost ratio in your annual board or owner review
step_description: Make fixed cost ratio a standing agenda item in your annual strategic review alongside revenue growth and gross margin. Presenting it alongside operating leverage trends over three to five years gives you and your stakeholders a clear picture of whether the business is becoming more or less scalable over time.

step_title: Calculate your exact interest coverage ratio today
step_description: Divide EBIT by your total monthly interest expense to determine how many times your earnings cover your interest obligations. A ratio below 1.5x means you are at serious risk of not servicing debt from operations. This number must be known before any other decision is made.

step_title: Call your bank before you miss a payment
step_description: Contact your primary lender this week and request an urgent meeting to discuss your debt position. Banks are dramatically more willing to restructure debt for clients who approach them proactively than for those who miss payments first. Prepare a 13-week cash flow forecast and a proposed repayment plan before the call.

step_title: Request a capital repayment holiday on all term loans
step_description: Formally apply for a 3–6 month capital repayment holiday across all term debt facilities. Most South African banks including ABSA, Standard Bank, Nedbank, and FNB have formal business distress restructuring programmes. A capital holiday reduces cash outflow while you restore EBIT — interest still accrues but the principal pause is critical relief.

step_title: Identify and sell non-core assets to reduce debt load
step_description: List every asset on your balance sheet that is not essential to generating current revenue — surplus equipment, unused vehicles, investment properties, dormant inventory. Liquidating even one significant asset can materially reduce your debt principal and the interest burden it generates. Target a 15–20% reduction in total debt within 90 days.

step_title: Halt all new debt-funded capital expenditure immediately
step_description: Place an immediate freeze on any new asset purchases, lease agreements, or capital commitments that would increase interest-bearing debt. Every additional rand of debt at this stage deepens the interest burden. Only reinstate capital expenditure once interest coverage exceeds 2.5x on a trailing three-month basis.

step_title: Explore refinancing high-rate debt at lower interest rates
step_description: List every debt facility with its current interest rate and remaining term. Identify the highest-rate facilities and approach alternative lenders — including SEFA, IDC, or alternative finance providers — for refinancing at lower rates. Even reducing your weighted average cost of debt by 2–3 percentage points meaningfully reduces monthly interest expense.

step_title: Drive EBIT growth to improve interest coverage from above
step_description: Interest burden improves both by reducing debt and by growing EBIT. Identify the fastest available route to a 20% EBIT improvement — price increases, cost cuts, or volume growth using existing capacity. A business with rising EBIT can service higher debt loads; the ratio improves from both ends simultaneously.

step_title: Convert short-term debt to long-term to reduce monthly pressure
step_description: If you have short-term facilities — overdrafts, bridging loans, credit cards — that are carrying long-term balances, negotiate their conversion to term loans with fixed monthly repayments over 3–5 years. This spreads the repayment burden, reduces monthly cash pressure, and often lowers your effective interest rate.

step_title: Explore equity injection to permanently reduce debt quantum
step_description: Consider whether a shareholder loan, external equity investor, or venture debt at lower rates could replace a portion of your high-cost bank debt. Equity does not carry interest. Even a partial equity injection that eliminates your highest-rate facility can shift the interest burden ratio from critical to manageable within one quarter.

step_title: Build a 24-month debt reduction roadmap with milestones
step_description: Once the immediate crisis is stabilised, create a structured 24-month plan targeting specific debt balances for elimination in priority order — highest rate first. Assign monthly surplus cash flow to debt reduction above minimum repayments. Reaching an interest coverage ratio of 3.0x or above should be your 18-month milestone.

step_title: Map every debt facility with rate, term, and monthly cost
step_description: Create a single-page debt register listing every facility — its outstanding balance, interest rate, monthly repayment, and maturity date. Most SME owners do not have this picture clearly in front of them. You cannot manage what you have not explicitly mapped, and this register is the foundation of every subsequent step.

step_title: Calculate interest coverage ratio and set a 3.0x target
step_description: Divide your trailing three-month average EBIT by your monthly interest expense to calculate your current coverage ratio. The widely accepted minimum safe level for an SME is 2.0x; a comfortable level is 3.0x or above. Use 3.0x as your improvement target and track monthly progress.

step_title: Renegotiate your highest-rate facility with your bank
step_description: Take your debt register to your bank and specifically request a rate review on your highest-rate facility. If your business has been performing and making payments on time, you have a legitimate case for a 1–2 percentage point reduction. In the current South African interest rate environment, proactive renegotiation is often successful.

step_title: Stop using revolving credit for long-term funding needs
step_description: Revolving credit facilities such as overdrafts and credit lines carry higher effective rates than term loans and are designed for short-term cash flow bridging, not long-term funding. If any revolving balance has been outstanding for more than six months, convert it to a term loan with a structured repayment schedule.

step_title: Allocate 20% of monthly free cash flow to debt reduction
step_description: Define a monthly debt reduction payment above your minimum repayments and automate it. Target 20% of free cash flow — cash remaining after operations and essential capex — directed to your highest-rate facility first. This approach, known as the avalanche method, minimises total interest paid over time.

step_title: Improve EBIT margin to grow coverage from the top line
step_description: Interest burden is a ratio of EBIT to interest, so improving EBIT directly improves the ratio without reducing debt. Identify two or three specific actions that could improve your EBIT margin by 3–5 percentage points over the next 90 days — a price increase, a cost reduction, or a product mix shift toward higher-margin lines.

step_title: Establish a debt ceiling policy before any new borrowing
step_description: Define a maximum debt-to-EBITDA ratio — typically 2.5x to 3.0x for a healthy SME — and enforce it as a financial governance rule. Any borrowing that would breach this ceiling requires explicit owner or board approval. This prevents the gradual debt accumulation that erodes interest burden ratios over time.

step_title: Explore SEFA or IDC funding to replace commercial bank debt
step_description: The Small Enterprise Finance Agency (SEFA) and the Industrial Development Corporation (IDC) offer SME funding at concessionary rates — often 2–5% below commercial bank rates. If your business qualifies, refinancing a portion of your commercial debt through these institutions can meaningfully reduce your interest burden.

step_title: Assess whether asset finance is cheaper than working capital debt
step_description: If you are using general working capital facilities to fund fixed assets, restructure this into dedicated asset finance — hire purchase or finance leases typically carry lower rates and match the asset useful life. Mismatching short-term debt with long-term assets is one of the most common causes of an elevated interest burden in SMEs.

step_title: Model the interest burden impact of your next growth investment
step_description: Before any new debt-funded investment, build a simple model showing the incremental EBIT the investment generates and whether it exceeds the incremental interest cost within 12 months. Only proceed with investments where the EBIT return is at least 3x the annual interest cost. This discipline prevents well-intentioned growth from worsening the ratio.

step_title: Document your current debt structure and cost of capital
step_description: Prepare a clean debt register showing every facility, its rate, term, security, and monthly cost. Calculate your weighted average cost of debt. This baseline document enables you to make rational financing decisions and protects against the gradual accumulation of sub-optimal debt that erodes a healthy interest burden over time.

step_title: Set a debt-to-EBITDA ceiling and review it annually
step_description: Formalise your maximum acceptable leverage level as a policy — most healthy SMEs target debt-to-EBITDA below 2.5x. Review your actual position against this ceiling annually or after any significant borrowing event. Having a policy prevents opportunistic borrowing from silently degrading your interest burden ratio.

step_title: Use your strong coverage ratio to negotiate better facility rates
step_description: A healthy interest coverage ratio is a negotiating asset. Approach your bank with your trailing 12-month financials and formally request a rate review across all facilities. Lenders price risk — a business with 4x+ coverage is a lower risk than their pricing may reflect, and you have grounds to request a 0.5–1.5% rate reduction.

step_title: Stress-test interest coverage against a 30% EBIT decline
step_description: Model your interest coverage ratio if EBIT dropped 30% due to a revenue shock, cost spike, or market disruption. If coverage falls below 1.5x in this scenario, you carry more debt risk than your healthy score suggests. Use this stress test to determine whether additional debt reduction or revenue diversification is warranted.

step_title: Evaluate whether debt can fund accretive growth investments
step_description: With a healthy interest burden, you have borrowing capacity that underperforming competitors may not. Identify one or two growth investments — equipment, acquisition, market expansion — where the projected return on investment exceeds your cost of debt by at least 3x. Disciplined use of debt at this stage is a competitive advantage.

step_title: Build an interest rate sensitivity model for your debt portfolio
step_description: If any of your debt is on variable rates, model the impact of a 1%, 2%, and 3% interest rate increase on your monthly interest expense and coverage ratio. South African prime rate has historically moved by 200–300 basis points in a single cycle. Knowing your exposure allows you to hedge or fix rates proactively.

step_title: Explore fixing variable rate debt ahead of rate cycle peaks
step_description: If the South African Reserve Bank is in a rate-hiking cycle, assess whether fixing your variable rate debt to a fixed rate provides protection. Fixed-rate facilities carry a slight premium but provide certainty — and prevent a rate cycle from converting a healthy interest burden into an at-risk position within 12 months.

step_title: Establish a revolving credit facility as emergency reserve
step_description: If you do not already have an undrawn revolving credit facility, negotiate one now while your financials are strong. Having R500 000 to R2 million in undrawn credit available costs very little when unused but provides critical liquidity insurance against unexpected cash shortfalls. Banks approve facilities to healthy businesses, not distressed ones.

step_title: Optimise debt maturity profile to avoid refinancing cliff risk
step_description: Review when your major debt facilities mature. If more than 40% of your total debt matures in the same 12-month window, you face refinancing cliff risk. Stagger maturities now by refinancing one facility early to spread renewal risk across different years.

step_title: Develop a capital structure strategy as part of annual planning
step_description: Include a formal capital structure review in your annual planning cycle — assess the right mix of debt, equity, and retained earnings to fund your three-year growth plan at the lowest cost and risk. A deliberate capital structure is one of the most underutilised levers in SME financial management.

step_title: Identify whether loss is operating or financing driven
step_description: Compare your operating margin to your net margin. If operating margin is positive but net margin is negative, your problem is debt cost or tax — not operations. If both are negative, you have a fundamental trading problem. This distinction determines your entire recovery strategy and must be answered before any other action.

step_title: Stop all cash outflows not essential to revenue generation
step_description: Issue an immediate spending freeze on all non-revenue-generating cash outflows. Every payment must be approved by the owner and tested against one question: does this directly protect or generate revenue this month? Discretionary spending at a critical net margin accelerates the path to insolvency.

step_title: Build a 13-week cash flow survival forecast today
step_description: Create a week-by-week cash forecast for the next 13 weeks listing every confirmed receipt and every committed payment. Use only confirmed receivables — not forecasted sales. This forecast tells you exactly when you will run out of cash and how much time you have to act. Update it every Monday without exception.

step_title: Raise prices on your top five products within seven days
step_description: Increase prices on your five highest-volume products or services by 10–20% immediately. Net margin deterioration is often a pricing problem as much as a cost problem. Even modest price increases on high-volume lines produce disproportionate net income improvement since all additional revenue above break-even flows to the bottom line.

step_title: Contact your bank immediately to restructure debt repayments
step_description: If financing costs are contributing to a negative net margin, contact your lender within 48 hours to request a capital repayment holiday or debt restructuring. A business with negative net margins generating positive EBIT has a financing problem, not a trading problem — and banks can and do restructure facilities for clients who engage them proactively.

step_title: Cut your total cost base by 25% within 60 days
step_description: Set a non-negotiable target of reducing your total cost base — COGS plus Opex plus financing costs — by 25% within 60 days. Work from the largest cost lines first. A 25% cost reduction at critical net margin typically moves the business from loss-making to break-even, buying time to rebuild revenue.

step_title: Exit or restructure every loss-making product or contract
step_description: Calculate the net profit contribution of every major product line and customer contract. Exit or restructure every arrangement generating a net loss — including all allocated overhead and financing costs. Continuing to operate loss-making lines while in a critical net margin position accelerates the deterioration of the whole business.

step_title: Engage a business rescue advisor to assess your options
step_description: If net margin has been negative for more than two consecutive quarters and your cash position is declining, engage a registered business rescue practitioner or turnaround specialist for an independent assessment. South Africa Companies Act provides formal business rescue procedures that can protect the business while a recovery plan is implemented. Early engagement preserves more options.

step_title: Accelerate collections on all outstanding debtors immediately
step_description: Call every debtor with an outstanding balance above R10 000 this week and request immediate payment or a firm commitment date. Offer a 2–3% early payment discount if necessary — the cost of the discount is lower than the cost of a deteriorating cash position. Net margin improvement requires both cost reduction and accelerated cash recovery.

step_title: Build a 12-month net margin recovery roadmap with monthly targets
step_description: Once immediate survival actions are in place, build a written 12-month recovery plan with monthly net margin targets, specific revenue and cost initiatives, and named owners for each action. Set a milestone of reaching positive net margin within 90 days and a target net margin of 5% or above within 12 months. Review weekly.

step_title: Decompose net margin into its four component drivers
step_description: Break your net margin into gross margin, Opex ratio, interest burden, and tax burden. Identify which component is most below benchmark for your industry. Targeted improvement on the weakest component delivers the fastest net margin recovery — and prevents you from spending effort on a driver that is already performing adequately.

step_title: Set a minimum net margin floor for all new business accepted
step_description: Define a minimum acceptable net margin percentage for any new contract, product line, or customer and enforce it as a business rule. Work backwards from your target net margin to determine the minimum gross margin required after deducting your Opex allocation, interest, and tax. Accepting below-floor business is the primary way at-risk businesses stay at-risk.

step_title: Implement a 5–8% price increase across your full product range
step_description: A 5% price increase on a business with a 5% net margin doubles net profit at the same volume — no additional costs required. Identify your least price-sensitive products and implement increases there first. Communicate increases with a value narrative and a reasonable notice period to minimise customer attrition.

step_title: Reduce total debt to lower net interest expense within 90 days
step_description: Identify the highest-rate debt facility and commit a defined monthly surplus — at minimum 15% of free cash flow — to reducing the principal. Lower principal means lower interest charges which flows directly to net margin improvement. Model the net margin impact of eliminating your most expensive facility within 12 months.

step_title: Review tax structure for legitimate rate reduction opportunities
step_description: Engage your tax advisor to review whether your current tax structure is optimal. Businesses at an at-risk net margin often have significant tax efficiency opportunities — SBC qualification, unclaimed deductions, or ETI credits — that are being overlooked.

step_title: Negotiate payment arrangements on your five largest outstanding invoices
step_description: For your five largest outstanding invoices, negotiate a structured payment arrangement — a specific amount due weekly or bi-weekly until the balance is cleared. A payment arrangement with a reliable customer is better than legal action that damages the relationship, delays cash, and incurs legal costs. Document all arrangements in writing and follow up religiously.

step_title: Implement COD or prepayment for all new orders immediately
step_description: Switch all new customer orders to cash on delivery or prepayment with immediate effect. Stop extending new credit while your existing debtors book is in crisis. Every new credit sale at a critical debtor days position adds to the working capital trap before the existing problem is resolved.

step_title: Instruct a debt collection attorney on all debtors over 90 days
step_description: For every customer whose invoice has been outstanding for more than 90 days and who has not responded to calls or demand letters, instruct a debt collection attorney or agency immediately. The probability of collection drops dramatically after 90 days — every additional day of delay reduces recovery prospects. Legal costs are typically recovered from the debtor if the claim is successful.

step_title: Write off irrecoverable debts and claim the tax deduction
step_description: Identify debts that are genuinely irrecoverable — debtors who are insolvent, untraceable, or where the cost of collection exceeds the amount owed — and write them off formally. Written-off bad debts are tax deductible in South Africa under Section 11(a) of the Income Tax Act. Writing them off clears your debtors book, improves the ratio, and generates a tax saving.

step_title: Implement a daily debtors report with 7-day collection targets
step_description: Create a daily debtors report showing every outstanding invoice with its age, amount, and a 7-day collection target. Review this report every morning. At a critical debtor days position, daily monitoring and daily action are non-negotiable. Weekly or monthly debtor reviews are insufficient when you are losing cash every day.

step_title: Redesign credit policy to prevent recurrence once crisis is resolved
step_description: Once the immediate debtors crisis is stabilised, redesign your credit policy from scratch — credit limits by customer, required credit checks for new accounts, maximum days before hold, escalation triggers, and collection procedures. A written credit policy prevents the structural issues that created the crisis from recurring. Implement within 90 days of crisis resolution.

step_title: Generate an aged debtors report and review it today
step_description: Pull a full aged debtors report showing every outstanding invoice by age bucket — current, 30 days, 60 days, 90 days, 90+ days. Calculate the percentage of your debtors book in each bucket. An at-risk debtors position typically has 20–40% of the book in the 60–90 day bucket — still recoverable but requiring urgent action.

step_title: Implement a weekly debtors collections process with named accountability
step_description: Assign a specific person to own debtor collections and set a weekly process — aged report reviewed Monday, calls made Tuesday through Thursday, escalations Friday. Collections performance should be measured against target debtor days monthly. Disciplined weekly process typically reduces debtor days by 10–15 days within 60 days without any structural change to credit policy.

step_title: Implement credit holds for all customers exceeding 45-day outstanding balance
step_description: Set up an automatic credit hold for all customers whose outstanding balance exceeds 45 days. No further orders should be processed until the overdue amount is paid or a payment arrangement is agreed. Credit holds create urgency for customers to pay and prevent the debtors position from worsening through continued trading on extended credit.

step_title: Run a credit check on all customers receiving more than 30-day terms
step_description: Conduct a credit bureau check on every customer currently receiving more than 30-day terms. Customers whose credit profile has deteriorated since you first extended terms represent an increasing collection risk. Adjust credit limits and terms for any customer whose credit score has declined materially — before their invoice becomes a bad debt.

step_title: Switch to same-day invoicing from delivery or completion
step_description: Eliminate any invoicing lag by issuing invoices on the same day as delivery or service completion. Many at-risk debtor positions have an invoicing lag of 3–7 days built in as standard practice. Removing this lag immediately reduces effective debtor days by the same amount at zero cost. Implement via mobile invoicing tools if field staff are doing the delivery.

step_title: Offer a 2% early payment discount to incentivise faster settlement
step_description: Introduce a 2% discount for payment within 7 days on all new invoices, communicated clearly on the invoice itself. A 2% discount for 23 days earlier payment has an effective annual cost of approximately 31% — high as a borrowing cost but very low compared to the working capital benefit of consistently faster collections.

step_title: Introduce progress billing for all projects over two weeks in duration
step_description: Require progress billing at defined milestones for any engagement running more than two weeks. Billing at 50% of project value at midpoint and 50% at completion can halve your effective debtor days on project revenue. Make progress billing a standard contractual term for all new engagements.

step_title: Explore invoice discounting as a working capital management tool
step_description: Assess whether a revolving invoice discounting facility — where you can selectively discount specific invoices when cash is needed — provides a cost-effective working capital buffer. Unlike full factoring, revolving invoice discounting gives you flexibility to use the facility only when needed, reducing the cost of the arrangement compared to discounting your entire book.

step_title: Formalise your credit policy in a written document
step_description: Write a formal credit policy covering: credit assessment criteria for new accounts, maximum credit limits by customer tier, required terms and conditions, escalation triggers, and collection procedures at 30, 45, 60, and 90 days. A written policy creates consistency, accountability, and defensibility — and reduces the debtor days that arise from informal or inconsistent credit decisions.

step_title: Set a 12-month debtor days target and track it monthly
step_description: Define a specific target debtor days figure — typically your invoice payment terms plus 5 days — and track your actual debtor days against this target monthly. Share the performance metric with your collections team and include it in monthly management accounts. What gets measured gets managed, and debtor days managed to a target consistently outperform those managed to a vague intention to improve.

step_title: Document your credit policy and collections process formally
step_description: Write down your current credit policy — credit assessment criteria, terms by customer tier, hold triggers, and collection procedures. A healthy debtor days position built on informal practices is fragile to staff changes. Documentation protects your current performance and provides a training foundation for new staff managing credit and collections.

step_title: Set a debtor days ceiling and configure monthly alerts
step_description: Define a maximum acceptable debtor days figure — your standard payment terms plus 5 days — and set up a monthly alert if actual debtor days exceed this ceiling for two consecutive months. Early warning prevents a healthy position from drifting to at-risk through gradual, unnoticed deterioration in collections discipline.

step_title: Assess whether debtor days can be reduced further through technology
step_description: Explore automated invoice delivery, payment reminders, and online payment portals that could reduce your average debtor days by 3–5 further days. On R10 million annual revenue, a 5-day reduction releases R137 000 in permanent working capital. Technology-enabled collections are more consistent and less resource-intensive than manual processes.

step_title: Run annual credit reviews on all major customer accounts
step_description: Conduct an annual review of the credit limits and terms extended to your top 20 accounts by outstanding balance. Reassess their creditworthiness using current financial information. Customer financial health changes — a customer who was creditworthy two years ago may not be today. Annual review prevents comfortable debtor relationships from becoming risky ones.

step_title: Explore whether a deposit or prepayment model suits your highest-risk accounts
step_description: Identify customers who represent the highest credit risk in your book — large balances, inconsistent payment history, or deteriorating financial health — and introduce a deposit or prepayment requirement for future orders. Migrating your highest-risk accounts to prepayment reduces the volatility of your debtors position without affecting your best customers.

step_title: Negotiate shorter payment terms with smaller, lower-credit customers
step_description: Review payment terms by customer size and credit quality. Large, creditworthy customers often command 30-day terms legitimately. Small customers with limited creditworthiness should be on shorter terms — 7 or 14 days — or COD. Tiering your credit terms by customer quality is the most risk-efficient approach to maintaining healthy debtor days.

step_title: Invest surplus working capital in yield-bearing short-term instruments
step_description: Your healthy debtor days generate surplus cash that many businesses leave idle. Move any cash surplus above your minimum operating buffer into a money market fund, 32-day notice account, or treasury product. Consistently healthy debtor management is a competitive advantage — ensure you are capturing the financial return it generates.

step_title: Stress-test debtors position against a customer concentration risk event
step_description: Model your debtor days and cash position if your largest customer delayed payment by 60 days. Identify whether this single event would push your debtors position to at-risk and what action you would take. Customer concentration in your debtors book is a specific risk worth understanding and planning for in advance.

step_title: Explore credit insurance for large individual debtor exposures
step_description: If any single customer represents more than 15–20% of your total debtors book, assess whether credit insurance on that exposure is cost-effective. Credit insurance pays out if the insured customer fails to pay due to insolvency or protracted default. Premiums are typically 0.2–0.5% of insured turnover — a low cost relative to the protection provided.

step_title: Include debtor days in your annual working capital strategy review
step_description: Make debtor days a standing agenda item in your annual financial planning cycle alongside inventory days and creditor days. Set targets for the coming year based on any changes to your customer mix, credit policy, or product offering. Debtors management that is reviewed and targeted annually consistently outperforms that managed only when problems emerge.

step_title: Assess whether critical creditor days reflects under-utilisation or over-payment
step_description: A critical creditor days score means you are paying suppliers too quickly relative to your working capital needs — you are funding your suppliers rather than optimising your own cash cycle. Calculate your current creditor days and compare to your invoice payment terms. If you are paying well before the due date, this is a cash management problem, not a supplier relationship one.

step_title: Stop all early supplier payments immediately
step_description: Issue a directive that no supplier invoice will be paid before its contractual due date. Many businesses default to paying invoices as they arrive rather than on due date — a practice that unnecessarily accelerates cash outflow. Paying on due date rather than early is an immediate improvement to creditor days that requires no negotiation.

step_title: Contact all major suppliers to negotiate extended payment terms
step_description: Call your five largest suppliers and request an extension of payment terms — from 30 to 60 days, or from 14 to 30 days. Present your purchase history, payment reliability, and projected volumes as leverage. A 30-day extension across your major suppliers can release weeks of cash flow equivalent to a significant working capital facility.

step_title: Negotiate 60-day terms as standard for all new supplier agreements
step_description: Make 60-day payment terms a non-negotiable requirement for all new supplier agreements. New suppliers entering a relationship are often more flexible on terms than established ones. Building longer terms into new contracts from the outset avoids the need to renegotiate later and immediately benefits your creditor days ratio.

step_title: Implement a formal payment run schedule to maximise terms utilisation
step_description: Set up a weekly or bi-weekly payment run schedule where all invoices are reviewed and payments are scheduled for the latest acceptable payment date. Ad-hoc payment of invoices as they arrive is a common cause of unnecessarily short creditor days. A scheduled payment run ensures you utilise your full terms on every supplier payment.

step_title: Request extended terms from your three largest spend categories
step_description: Prioritise your renegotiation effort on the three supplier categories representing the most spend. A 30-day extension from your three largest cost categories will improve overall creditor days more than a 30-day extension from ten small suppliers. Concentrate negotiating effort where the cash impact is greatest.

step_title: Offer volume commitments in exchange for extended payment terms
step_description: Approach key suppliers with a formal volume commitment — a guaranteed annual purchase quantity — in exchange for extended payment terms of 60–90 days. Volume certainty is valuable to most suppliers and can offset the cost to them of extended terms. Document the commitment clearly to make it a tradeable business arrangement.

step_title: Explore supply chain finance for your largest supplier relationships
step_description: Research supply chain finance programmes — available through several South African banks — where the bank pays your supplier on due date and you repay the bank on extended terms of 90–120 days. This provides your supplier with certainty of payment while giving you significantly extended creditor days. It is a structured, bank-facilitated extension of your creditor cycle.

step_title: Benchmark creditor days against your sector and set an improvement target
step_description: Research creditor days benchmarks for your sector — retail typically achieves 45–60 days, manufacturing 30–45 days, services 20–30 days. If your creditor days are significantly below your sector benchmark, you are funding your working capital cycle more expensively than your competitors. Set a specific target to close the gap within 12 months.

step_title: Build a supplier terms management calendar for all major contracts
step_description: Create a calendar showing every major supplier contract, its current payment terms, and the next opportunity to renegotiate. Schedule a renegotiation conversation 60 days before each contract renewal. Systematic management of supplier terms through a calendar converts a reactive creditor days position into a proactively managed competitive advantage.

step_title: Audit current payment terms across all major suppliers
step_description: List every major supplier with its current contractual payment terms, your actual average payment date, and the cash impact of paying on due date versus current practice. Many at-risk creditor days positions exist because businesses pay before the contractual due date by default. Identifying where you are paying early is the first step to correcting it.

step_title: Implement a structured payment run to use terms in full
step_description: Set up a bi-weekly payment run where all invoices are reviewed and scheduled for payment on — not before — their contractual due date. Centralise payment authority so that ad-hoc early payments require explicit approval. This single discipline improvement often adds 7–14 days to effective creditor days without any supplier negotiation.

step_title: Renegotiate terms with your three largest suppliers to 45–60 days
step_description: Approach your three largest suppliers and request an extension of payment terms to 45–60 days. Present your purchase history, payment reliability, and projected growth as the basis for the request. Even if only one of three agrees, the cash impact is immediate and meaningful. Prioritise your largest spend categories for the greatest working capital benefit.

step_title: Make 45-day minimum terms a requirement for all new supplier agreements
step_description: Establish 45-day payment terms as your minimum standard requirement for all new supplier agreements. New suppliers are almost always more flexible on terms during contract negotiation than established ones. Building longer terms into new agreements from day one avoids the need for subsequent renegotiation and benefits your creditor days immediately.

step_title: Track creditor days monthly alongside debtor and inventory days
step_description: Add creditor days to your monthly management accounts as part of a working capital dashboard alongside debtor days and inventory days. Monthly visibility of all three components makes it easy to see the combined impact on your cash conversion cycle and identify which element needs the most attention.

step_title: Offer volume commitments to suppliers in exchange for extended terms
step_description: Identify suppliers where a formal volume commitment over 12 months would be valuable to them in exchange for extended payment terms. A guaranteed volume offer reduces a supplier's sales uncertainty and justifies the cost of extending your terms. Structure the offer as a formal written agreement to give it commercial weight.

step_title: Evaluate consolidating suppliers to earn longer terms through higher volume
step_description: If you are spreading spend across many small suppliers, consolidating to fewer larger suppliers concentrates volume and increases your leverage to negotiate longer terms. A supplier receiving 100% of your category spend has more reason to extend 60-day terms than one receiving 20%. Supplier consolidation is a strategic lever for improving creditor days.

step_title: Benchmark creditor days against your sector median
step_description: Research creditor days benchmarks for your industry and compare your current performance. If you are below sector median, your competitors are effectively funding their working capital more cheaply than you. Closing the gap to sector median through better terms management is a free improvement to your cash conversion cycle.

step_title: Explore supply chain finance for your largest supplier relationships
step_description: Research supply chain finance programmes available through South African banks. Under these programmes, the bank pays your supplier promptly while you repay the bank on extended terms — effectively extending your creditor days without impacting your supplier's cash flow. This is a win-win arrangement that benefits both parties.

step_title: Set a 12-month creditor days improvement target by supplier category
step_description: Define a 12-month creditor days target for each major supplier category — materials, services, utilities, subcontractors — and build the specific negotiation and terms management actions required to reach it. Category-level targets are more actionable than a single blended number and produce faster results through focused negotiation.

step_title: Document your current supplier terms and payment schedule
step_description: Record every major supplier with its contracted payment terms, actual average payment date, and creditor days contribution. This baseline protects your healthy creditor days from eroding when staff change and ensures your payment run schedule consistently utilises the full terms available rather than defaulting to early payment.

step_title: Maintain your payment run discipline to protect terms utilisation
step_description: Reinforce your bi-weekly or weekly payment run as a standing operational discipline. The most common cause of healthy creditor days drifting to at-risk is the return to ad-hoc early payment driven by supplier pressure or staff convenience. Maintain centralised payment authority and the run schedule as a non-negotiable process.

step_title: Use strong payment history to negotiate better terms at renewal
step_description: Your consistent on-time payment history is a negotiating asset. When major supplier contracts come up for renewal, request an extension of payment terms — from 45 to 60 days or from 30 to 45 days — as part of the renewal discussion. Present your payment track record as the basis for the request. Suppliers value reliable payers and will often extend terms to retain them.

step_title: Ensure new supplier agreements include minimum 45-day terms
step_description: Set 45-day payment terms as your standard minimum for all new supplier agreements. Protect your healthy creditor days from erosion by new suppliers offering only 14 or 30-day terms as a default. Negotiate at contract initiation — it is far easier to secure favourable terms when establishing a new relationship than to extend them after the relationship is set.

step_title: Explore whether 60–90 day terms are achievable for major supplier categories
step_description: Assess whether your highest-spend supplier categories could be extended to 60 or 90 days through volume commitments, supply chain finance, or strategic partnership arrangements. Even moving from 45 to 60 days on your largest category releases meaningful additional working capital permanently and reduces your CCC further.

step_title: Include creditor days in your annual working capital review
step_description: Make creditor days a standing item in your annual financial planning cycle. Review every major supplier contract for terms optimisation opportunities at renewal, assess whether consolidation would improve leverage, and confirm that your payment run discipline is being maintained. Annual reviews prevent silent erosion of a healthy creditor days position.

step_title: Explore dynamic discounting for early payment on selective invoices
step_description: Investigate dynamic discounting platforms that allow you to offer early payment on selected supplier invoices in exchange for a discount — only when you have surplus cash and the discount yield exceeds your money market return. Dynamic discounting turns your cash surplus into a managed yield opportunity rather than an early payment donation to your supplier.

step_title: Stress-test creditor days against a supplier relationship disruption
step_description: Model what happens to your working capital cycle if your two largest suppliers reduced terms from 60 to 30 days simultaneously — a plausible scenario during a sector credit crunch or if those suppliers face their own cash pressures. Identify the cash impact and your response plan. Diversifying supplier relationships is a key risk mitigation in this scenario.

step_title: Build supplier relationship strength to protect long-term terms
step_description: Invest in strategic supplier relationships beyond transactional purchasing — share your growth plans, provide forecast visibility, pay reliably, and give feedback. Suppliers who view you as a strategic partner rather than a commodity customer are more likely to maintain favourable terms during market disruptions and more likely to offer improved terms as your volume grows.

step_title: Include creditor days strategy in your three-year working capital plan
step_description: Dedicate a section of your three-year business plan to creditor days strategy — identifying target terms by supplier category at each revenue milestone, the supplier consolidation and relationship investments required, and the working capital benefit from each improvement. Proactive creditor management at scale is a CFO-level discipline that generates real competitive advantage in capital efficiency.

step_title: Map every active WIP job with its start date and cost to date
step_description: Create a complete list of every job, project, or batch currently in work-in-progress, with its start date, total costs incurred, expected completion date, and billed amount to date. At a critical WIP days ratio, cash is trapped in uncompleted work — you cannot release it until jobs are completed and invoiced. This map tells you exactly how much cash is trapped and where.

step_title: Prioritise completion of highest-value WIP jobs within seven days
step_description: Rank all WIP jobs by value and direct all available resources to completing the highest-value jobs as quickly as possible. Each completed job converts WIP to a billable invoice — releasing trapped cash. In a critical WIP days position, completion velocity is a cash flow lever. Assign overtime, additional resources, or management oversight to the top five jobs by value.

step_title: Invoice immediately upon each job completion — no batch billing
step_description: Implement a policy that every job or deliverable is invoiced on the day it is completed or accepted by the customer. Batch billing — invoicing weekly or at month-end — adds 7–31 days of unnecessary delay between completion and cash receipt. Every day between completion and invoicing is a day of WIP days that has already been resolved but not yet captured.

step_title: Introduce progress billing on all jobs longer than two weeks
step_description: Implement a mandatory progress billing policy for all new jobs expected to take longer than two weeks — billing 30% at commencement, 40% at midpoint, and 30% at completion. Progress billing converts long-duration WIP into a series of shorter billing cycles, dramatically reducing the cash trapped in work in progress at any point in time.

step_title: Identify and resolve all WIP jobs stalled by customer or internal delays
step_description: Review every WIP job that has been open for more than your target completion cycle and identify the specific cause of delay — customer non-responsiveness, internal resource bottleneck, or scope dispute. Escalate each stalled job personally and set a 48-hour deadline for resolution. Stalled WIP is one of the most expensive forms of working capital trap because it also consumes management capacity.

step_title: Require deposits of 30–50% before commencing any new work
step_description: Implement a mandatory deposit requirement of 30–50% before commencing any new job or project. Deposits fund a portion of the initial costs, reducing the WIP that accumulates before the first billing milestone. Communicate this as standard business practice and hold firm — customers who refuse a reasonable deposit are often the same ones who delay final payment.

step_title: Set a maximum WIP days limit per job and enforce it operationally
step_description: Define a maximum number of days any single job may remain in WIP before a billing milestone must be reached. For example, no job may accumulate more than 30 days of unbilled WIP. Assign the operations or project manager the responsibility to flag any job approaching this limit. This operational limit prevents runaway WIP accumulation on individual jobs.

step_title: Stop accepting new jobs until existing WIP backlog is cleared
step_description: If your WIP backlog is so large that resources are stretched and completion dates are slipping, consider a temporary moratorium on accepting new work until existing WIP is reduced to a manageable level. Continuing to start new jobs while existing ones remain uncompleted compounds the WIP days problem and delays cash receipt on all jobs simultaneously.

step_title: Implement weekly WIP reporting with completion and billing targets
step_description: Set up a weekly WIP dashboard showing all active jobs with their start date, estimated completion, costs incurred, amount billed, and amount outstanding. Review this every Monday and set specific completion and billing targets for the week. Weekly WIP management reduces average WIP days by 20–30% within 60 days in most service and project businesses.

step_title: Redesign your service delivery model to shorten job cycle times
step_description: Assess whether your standard job or project structure can be redesigned to reduce cycle times — breaking large projects into smaller discrete deliverables, standardising recurring job types, or improving resource allocation between jobs. Shorter cycle times reduce peak WIP at any point in time and improve overall WIP days structurally rather than just tactically.

step_title: Generate a WIP age analysis and identify stalled jobs
step_description: List all active WIP jobs with their start date, current age, costs incurred, and billing status. Flag any job that has been in WIP for more than 50% of its expected duration without a billing milestone reached. At-risk WIP days typically has a cluster of stalled or slow-moving jobs that are anchoring the overall ratio upward.

step_title: Implement progress billing for all new jobs over 14 days
step_description: Require progress billing at defined milestones for all new engagements expected to run more than 14 days. Billing at 30–50% at midpoint and the remainder on completion reduces peak WIP by approximately half on each job. Implement this immediately for all new engagements and negotiate it into existing jobs at the next natural checkpoint.

step_title: Resolve all stalled WIP jobs within 14 days
step_description: For every job that has been open for more than its expected completion time, make a direct call to the client or responsible person and set a 14-day resolution deadline — either complete and invoice, or formally close and bill for work done to date. Stalled jobs are the primary driver of at-risk WIP days and must be resolved before they age further.

step_title: Switch from month-end billing to completion-date billing
step_description: If your billing cycle is monthly, switch to invoicing on the day of job completion or milestone sign-off. Monthly billing adds an average of 15 days of unnecessary WIP delay across all jobs completed in mid-month.
